claim: Aspirin intake leads to an up to twofold reduction in colorectal adenoma incidence rates at higher doses.
source: Aspirin intake has been shown to lead to significant protection against colorectal cancer, for example with an up to twofold reduction in colorectal adenoma incidence rates at higher doses.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by references to epidemiological studies throughout the manuscript.

claim: Aspirin reduces the rate of tumor cell division.
source: in vitro and in vivo experiments have recently shown that aspirin can also have a direct effect on cellular kinetics and fitness. It reduces the rate of tumor cell division and increases the rate of cell death.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous experimental work cited in the manuscript (Shimura et al., 2020; Zumwalt et al., 2017).

claim: Aspirin increases the rate of cell death.
source: in vitro and in vivo experiments have recently shown that aspirin can also have a direct effect on cellular kinetics and fitness. It reduces the rate of tumor cell division and increases the rate of cell death.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous experimental work cited in the manuscript (Shimura et al., 2020; Zumwalt et al., 2017).

claim: Only a model that included colonic crypt competition can account for the observed age-incidence curve.
source: Fitting the predictions to age incidence data revealed that only a model that included colonic crypt competition can account for the observed age-incidence curve.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical modeling and fitting to epidemiological data as shown in the Results section.

claim: Changes in cellular fitness within experimentally observed ranges could reduce advanced adenoma incidence by a sufficient amount to account for age incidence data in aspirin-treated patient cohorts.
source: We found that changes in cellular fitness that were within the experimentally observed ranges could reduce advanced adenoma incidence by a sufficient amount to account for age incidence data in aspirin-treated patient cohorts.
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational modeling using experimentally measured parameters.

claim: Colorectal cancer currently affects about 5% of the population in the USA.
source: Colorectal cancer currently affects about 5% of the population in the USA and is a major cause of cancer-related deaths (Siegel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2020.

claim: Aspirin is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) and is a cyclo-oxygenase (COX)–2 inhibitor.
source: Aspirin is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) and is a cyclo-oxygenase (COX)–2 inhibitor (Goel et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The CAPP2 trial demonstrated that the intake of 600 mg of aspirin per day for 2 years resulted in a 63% reduction in colorectal cancer incidence in Lynch Syndrome patients.
source: The CAPP2 trial Burn et al., 2011 demonstrated that the intake of 600 mg of aspirin per day for 2 years resulted in a 63% reduction in colorectal cancer incidence in Lynch Syndrome patients.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the CAPP2 trial cited in the manuscript.

claim: Observation of the protective effect of aspirin required a follow-up time of more than 55 months.
source: Interestingly, observation of the protective effect of aspirin required a follow-up time of more than 55 months (Burn et al., 2011).
evidence: This is reported from the CAPP2 trial.

claim: Studies report a reduction in cancer or adenoma incidence of the order of 10–50% in aspirin-treated compared to placebo groups, depending on the exact dose and frequency of aspirin intake.
source: These studies report a reduction in cancer or adenoma incidence of the order of 10–50% in aspirin-treated compared to placebo groups, depending on the exact dose and frequency of aspirin intake.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Inflammation is a possible driver of colorectal carcinogenesis.
source: Inflammation is a possible driver of colorectal carcinogenesis (Itzkowitz and Yio, 2004), and aspirin can reduce the extent of inflammation in the cellular microenvironment, which might contribute to a reduced development of disease.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Itzkowitz and Yio, 2004.

claim: Aspirin can reduce the extent of inflammation in the cellular microenvironment, which might contribute to a reduced development of disease.
source: Inflammation is a possible driver of colorectal carcinogenesis (Itzkowitz and Yio, 2004), and aspirin can reduce the extent of inflammation in the cellular microenvironment, which might contribute to a reduced development of disease.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by the anti-inflammatory properties of aspirin.

claim: The composition of the colorectal microbiome determines the degree of protection provided by aspirin.
source: Other microenvironmental effects, such as the composition of the colorectal microbiome (Prizment et al., 2020; Brennan et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2020), have also been shown to determine the degree of protection provided by aspirin.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies on the microbiome and aspirin.

claim: Physiologically relevant aspirin concentrations can have a direct effect on tumor cells, reducing their rate of proliferation and increasing their death rate.
source: Our previous in vitro and in vivo work, however, has shown that physiologically relevant aspirin concentrations can have a direct effect on tumor cells, reducing their rate of proliferation and increasing their death rate (Shimura et al., 2020; Zumwalt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on the authors' own experimental work.

claim: Aspirin can lead to a lower probability that newly generated tumor cells successfully give rise to clonal expansion, thus increasing the likelihood that these initially transformed cells go extinct.
source: This not only results in reduced tumor growth, but can also lead to a lower probability that newly generated tumor cells successfully give rise to clonal expansion, thus increasing the likelihood that these initially transformed cells go extinct (Wodarz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from previous modeling work by the authors.

claim: The model assumes two early molecular events: an inactivation of the APC gene and an activation of the KRAS oncogene.
source: There are two early molecular events that we postulate (without assuming their temporal order): (1) An inactivation of the APC gene, or a related event that affects the functioning of the beta-catenin/WNT signaling pathway, and (2) an activation of the KRAS oncogene (or another gain-of-function mutation).
evidence: This is an explicit assumption of the mathematical model.

claim: The inactivation of the APC tumor suppressor gene requires two molecular events, corresponding to the inactivation of the two copies of the gene.
source: The inactivation of the APC tumor suppressor gene is a classic example of a loss-of-function mutation, which implies two molecular events, corresponding to the inactivation of the two copies of the gene.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tumor suppressor genes.

claim: The mutation rate for APC inactivation is assumed to be u = 10–7 per cell division.
source: The associated mutation rate is therefore assumed to be u = 10–7 per cell division.
evidence: This is a parameter assumption based on literature values.

claim: The mutation rate for KRAS activation is about two orders of magnitude lower than APC inactivation (μ = 10–9 per cell division).
source: The activation of the KRAS oncogene, on the other hand, is a gain-of-function event, whose mutation rate is about two orders of magnitude lower (μ = 10–9 per cell division).
evidence: This is a parameter assumption based on literature values.

claim: The presence of the APC-/- genotype has been related to the appearance of early adenomas.
source: The presence of the APC-/- genotype has been related to the appearance of early adenomas (type 3) (Armaghany et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Armaghany et al., 2012.

claim: Cells that have not inactivated APC but are characterized by KRAS activation have been linked to aberrant crypt foci.
source: Cells that have not inactivated APC but are characterized by KRAS activation (types 4 and 5) have been linked to aberrant crypt foci (Pretlow and Pretlow, 2005; Jass, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pretlow and Pretlow, 2005 and Jass, 2006.

claim: The combination of APC-/- and KRAS+ mutations is thought to correlate with the growth of advanced adenomas.
source: The combination of both types of mutations (type 6) is thought to correlate with the growth of advanced adenomas (Armaghany et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Armaghany et al., 2012.

claim: Among non-hypermutated colorectal tumors, KRAS was mutated in only about 43% of patient samples.
source: For example, it has been reported that among non-hypermutated colorectal tumors, KRAS was mutated in only about 43% of patient samples (Network, 2012), indicating the importance of a variety of evolutionary pathways.
evidence: This is data from The Cancer Genome Atlas Network study.

claim: A linear model that did not include inter-crypt competition was rejected because its best fits corresponded to zero crypt fission rates.
source: We first attempted to fit the model in the absence of crypt competition (KR = KA = ∞), by varying the SC division rate within the physiological range and finding the best fitting value for crypt fission rates. The best fitting parameter combinations always corresponded to zero crypt fission rates.
evidence: This is a finding from the model fitting procedure.

claim: Non-zero crypt fission rates resulted in a much steeper rise in the adenoma incidence compared to that reported in Brenner et al., 2014.
source: Non-zero crypt fission rates resulted in a much steeper rise in the adenoma incidence compared to that reported in Brenner et al., 2014.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing model predictions to epidemiological data.

claim: Including crypt competition in the model resolved the issue of unrealistically steep rise in incidence.
source: Including crypt competition in the model has resolved this issue.
evidence: This is demonstrated through model fitting results.

claim: For the model that includes crypt competition, it was possible to find nearly equally good fits for a range of biologically plausible parameter values.
source: For the model that includes crypt competition, it was possible to find nearly equally good fits for a range of biologically plausible parameter values, see Figure 2.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2 showing fitting results.

claim: The likelihood of the APC pathway versus KRAS pathway is determined by the crypt fission rates, and not by mutation rates or crypt conversion rates.
source: We found, consistent with (Paterson et al., 2020), that the likelihood of each of these two pathways is determined by the crypt fission rates, and not by mutation rates or crypt conversion rates (Figure 3(d)); in addition, it is sensitive of the carrying capacity parameters, KA and KR.
evidence: This is demonstrated through model analysis and shown in Figure 3(d).

claim: For the biologically relevant parameter group where the carrying capacity associated with type 3 (APC-/-,KRAS-) is larger, the pathway through the inactivation of the APC gene is predominant.
source: We observe that for the biologically relevant group where the carrying capacity associated with type 3 (APC-/-,KRAS-) is larger, the pathway through the inactivation of the APC gene is predominant.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3(c) and is consistent with findings from Paterson et al., 2020.

claim: In the model, the number of type 3 (APC-/-,KRAS-) crypts is in the hundreds while type 5 (APC-/+,KRAS+) crypts are relatively rare.
source: We observe that in the model, the number of type 3 (APC-/-,KRAS-) crypts is in the hundreds while type 5 (APC-/+,KRAS+) crypts are relatively rare.
evidence: This is shown in Appendix 1—figures 12 and 13.

claim: Sulindac inhibited the fission of APC-deficient crypts and thus reduced adenoma numbers in mice.
source: In other work, it has also been demonstrated that a related non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, sulindac, inhibited the fission of APC-deficient crypts and thus reduced adenoma numbers in mice.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fischer et al., 2014.

claim: The model predictions are consistent with the observed bounds: for the aspirin dose that corresponds to 6–14 tablets per week, the predicted relative risk ranges between about 0.35 and 0.80, depending on the age when aspirin was administered.
source: Comparing this with the relative advanced adenoma risk plot in Figure 4(d), we can see that the model predictions are consistent with the observed bounds: for the aspirin dose that corresponds to 6–14 tablets per week (referred to as high dose, Figure 4(d)), the predicted relative risk ranges between about 0.35 and 0.80, depending on the age when aspirin was administered.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing model predictions in Figure 4(d) with data from Chan et al., 2004.

claim: The effect of aspirin decreases with smaller doses, resulting in the relative risk for intermediate doses varying roughly in the 0.6–0.9 range.
source: Consistently with (Chan et al., 2004), we found that the effect of aspirin decreases with smaller doses, resulting in the relative risk for intermediate doses varying roughly in the 0.6–0.9 range (brown bars in Figure 4(d)), while for the light dose it varied in the 0.8–0.9 range (blue bars in Figure 4(d)).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4(d) and is consistent with Chan et al., 2004.

claim: Including aspirin's effect on inter-crypt (fission/death) dynamics is essential to explain the data.
source: This suggests that including aspirin's effect on inter-crypt (fission/death) dynamics is essential to explain the data, which makes intuitive sense because crypt dynamics are thought to be drivers of disease development.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Appendix 1—figure 15 where only intra-crypt effects resulted in minimal risk reduction.

claim: Risk reduction clearly depends on the age of the patients when aspirin was administered.
source: We observe that risk reduction clearly depends on the age of the patients when aspirin was administered. As we see in Figure 4(d), the relative risk can be as low as about 0.4 for patients that started treatment at age 20 and assessed at age 30, compared to a more modest reduction to relative risk of 0.8 for patients receiving treatment later in life
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4(d).

claim: Aspirin-induced risk reduction, as predicted by this model, does not disappear even decades after aspirin treatment stopped.
source: Further, we will mention that aspirin-induced risk reduction, as predicted by this model, does not disappear even decades after aspirin treatment stopped (Figure 4(b)).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model simulations.

claim: The inclusion of a relatively slow growth of the adenoma significantly changed numerical values of the fitted parameters.
source: While stopping the simulations once the first type-6 crypt is produced leads to qualitatively similar results, the inclusion of a relatively slow growth of the adenoma significantly changed numerical values of the fitted parameters.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing different modeling approaches.

claim: Changes in cellular fitness that were within the experimentally observed ranges can lead to significant reductions in predicted late adenoma incidence, which are consistent with the epidemiologically observed reductions (ranging between 10–50%).
source: The mathematical analysis demonstrated that parameter changes of a magnitude that lies within our experimentally observed range can lead to significant reductions in predicted late adenoma incidence, which are consistent with the epidemiologically observed reductions (ranging between 10–50%, Chan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the modeling study comparing predictions to epidemiological data.

claim: The aspirin-induced changes in cellular fitness that were observed experimentally can in principle explain a significant portion of the protective effect observed on the population level.
source: We can conclude that the aspirin-induced changes in cellular fitness that we observed experimentally can in principle explain a significant portion of the protective effect observed on the population level.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the study based on model predictions.

claim: The ASPREE trial found that cancer incidence was not significantly changed by aspirin in a cohort of older individuals (70 years or older).
source: This trial investigated the effect of aspirin treatment in a cohort of older individuals, 70 years or older without cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability. It was found that cancer incidence was not significantly changed by aspirin, but that the aspirin-treated group experienced a higher rate of cancer-induced mortality.
evidence: This is reported from the ASPREE trial (McNeil et al., 2018; McNeil et al., 2021).

claim: The ASPREE trial found that the aspirin-treated group experienced a higher rate of cancer-induced mortality.
source: It was found that cancer incidence was not significantly changed by aspirin, but that the aspirin-treated group experienced a higher rate of cancer-induced mortality.
evidence: This is reported from the ASPREE trial (McNeil et al., 2018; McNeil et al., 2021).

claim: The absence of a significant effect of aspirin on cancer incidence in the ASPREE study is consistent with the model predictions that the effect of aspirin treatment on cancer incidence diminished when treatment was initiated in older ages.
source: The absence of a significant effect of aspirin on cancer incidence in this study is consistent with our model predictions. Our mathematical analysis demonstrated that the effect of aspirin treatment on cancer incidence diminished when treatment was initiated in older ages.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ASPREE results in light of the model predictions.

claim: By the time the tumor has reached a given size, it will have undergone more cell divisions under aspirin treatment compared to the placebo group.
source: As the established tumors continue to grow during aspirin treatment, they likely do so with altered kinetics (reduced division rates and increased death rates, leading to a higher turnover). This means that by the time the tumor has reached a given size (e.g. at which it becomes clinically detectable), it will have undergone more cell divisions under aspirin treatment compared to the placebo group.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the kinetic effects of aspirin.

claim: The aspirin-treated tumor might be more virulent and less responsive to therapies, resulting in more deaths.
source: Hence, the tumor will on average have accumulated more mutations once this detectable tumor size is reached. This in turn means that the aspirin-treated tumor might be more virulent and less responsive to therapies, resulting in more deaths.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the ASPREE mortality findings based on theoretical reasoning.

claim: Upon detection, an aspirin-treated tumor is more evolved than a tumor that grows without aspirin.
source: The theoretically derived notion that upon detection, an aspirin-treated tumor is more evolved than a tumor that grows without aspirin (Wodarz et al., 2017) is supported by the ASPREE analysis, which found that aspirin-treated patients were more likely to have metastasized cancers and stage 4 cancers compared to the placebo group (McNeil et al., 2018; McNeil et al., 2021).
evidence: This theoretical prediction from Wodarz et al., 2017 is supported by findings from the ASPREE trial.

claim: ASPREE analysis found that aspirin-treated patients were more likely to have metastasized cancers and stage 4 cancers compared to the placebo group.
source: The theoretically derived notion that upon detection, an aspirin-treated tumor is more evolved than a tumor that grows without aspirin (Wodarz et al., 2017) is supported by the ASPREE analysis, which found that aspirin-treated patients were more likely to have metastasized cancers and stage 4 cancers compared to the placebo group (McNeil et al., 2018; McNeil et al., 2021).
evidence: This is data from the ASPREE trial analysis.

claim: The model contains six different cell populations, denoted as types 1 through 6.
source: The associated selection-mutation diagram is shown in Figure 1 and contains six different cell populations, denoted as types 1 through 6.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1.

claim: The populations occupying the top row (types 1–3) are characterized by an unmutated KRAS oncogene.
source: The populations occupying the top row (types 1–3) are characterized by an unmutated KRAS oncogene; the populations of the bottom row (types 4–6) all have the KRAS mutation activated.
evidence: This is part of the model definition shown in Figure 1.

claim: The populations of the bottom row (types 4–6) all have the KRAS mutation activated.
source: The populations occupying the top row (types 1–3) are characterized by an unmutated KRAS oncogene; the populations of the bottom row (types 4–6) all have the KRAS mutation activated.
evidence: This is part of the model definition shown in Figure 1.

claim: Moving from left to right on the diagram, the number of inactivated copies of the APC gene increases from 0 to 2.
source: Moving from left to right on this diagram, the number of inactivated copies of the APC gene increases from 0 to 2, such that populations of types 1 and 4 are APC+/+, populations of types 2 and 5 are both APC+/-, and populations of types 3 and 6 are APC-/-.
evidence: This is part of the model definition shown in Figure 1.

claim: The model assumes flexibility regarding the order with which the different mutations can occur.
source: As in the previous study (Paterson et al., 2020), we assume flexibility regarding the order with which the different mutations can occur. Hence, it is assumed that the initial mutation can occur either in APC or in KRAS.
evidence: This is an explicit assumption of the model.

claim: Some studies indicate that an initial mutation in KRAS leads to the formation of non-dysplastic polyps, which could represent an evolutionary dead end for neoplasias.
source: Some studies indicate that an initial mutation in KRAS leads to the formation of non-dysplastic polyps, which could represent an evolutionary dead end for neoplasias (Jen et al., 1994; Chan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jen et al., 1994 and Chan et al., 2003.

claim: It has been suggested that an initial KRAS mutation might be able to drive the initiation of colorectal carcinogenesis.
source: On the other hand, it has been suggested that an initial KRAS mutation might be able to drive the initiation of colorectal carcinogenesis (Jass, 2006; Pretlow and Pretlow, 2005), based on mutation frequencies in aberrant crypt foci and adenomas.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jass, 2006 and Pretlow and Pretlow, 2005.

claim: The model uses a colonic crypt as a basic unit.
source: We model the population dynamics of the colon by using a colonic crypt as a basic unit, which is similar in concept to recently published work (Paterson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an explicit modeling assumption.

claim: There are very few stem cells per crypt.
source: Once it was discovered that there were very few stem cells per crypt (Nicholson et al., 2018; Humphries and Wright, 2008), it became clear that the evolutionary dynamics can be conveniently described at the level of crypts, because crypts are likely to be homogeneous with respect to the driver mutations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nicholson et al., 2018 and Humphries and Wright, 2008.

claim: Crypts are likely to be homogeneous with respect to the driver mutations.
source: Once it was discovered that there were very few stem cells per crypt (Nicholson et al., 2018; Humphries and Wright, 2008), it became clear that the evolutionary dynamics can be conveniently described at the level of crypts, because crypts are likely to be homogeneous with respect to the driver mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the small number of stem cells per crypt.

claim: Cell types APC+/-, APC-/-, and KRAS + all have a selective advantage compared to the wild type.
source: Cell types APC+/-, APC-/-, and KRAS + all have a selective advantage compared to the wild type, which we assume results in an increase of the SC division rate (see Section 2 of Appendix 1 for details).
evidence: This is a modeling assumption based on biological knowledge.

claim: Modified crypts of types APC-/- and KRAS + have been reported to undergo crypt fission.
source: Modified crypts of types APC-/- and KRAS + have been reported to undergo crypt fission; in other words, while the total population of a single crypt remains constant (even though it is populated by SCs that are fitter than the wild-type SCs), the crypt can undergo a doubling, thus increasing the total number of such modified crypts.
evidence: This is supported by literature references cited in the manuscript.

claim: The fission rates of different crypt types have been reported in the literature.
source: The fission rates of different crypt types have been reported in the literature (Paterson et al., 2020; Nicholson et al., 2018; Humphries et al., 2013; Baker et al., 2014) and are denoted by γi
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The probability to have produced a single crypt of type 6 by time t is denoted by P(t).
source: The probability to have produced a single crypt of type 6 (the APC-/-KRAS+ phenotype) by time t is denoted by P(t) and is approximated by the following equation Chou and Wang, 2015
evidence: This is part of the mathematical model formulation.

claim: At the time of detection, an advanced adenoma is characterized by a certain size, N.
source: We further assume that crypts of type 6 engage in a fission-death dynamics (with the corresponding rates γ6 and δ6). At the time of detection, an advanced adenoma is characterized by a certain size, N.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption.

claim: The approximations were checked against stochastic (Gillespie) simulations recording the incidence of size N colonies of type 6 crypts, yielding excellent agreement.
source: These approximations were checked against stochastic (Gillespie) simulations recording the incidence of size N colonies of type 6 crypts, yielding excellent agreement (see Section 5 of Appendix 1 for details).
evidence: This is a validation of the mathematical approximations.

claim: The relative risk for adenoma was 0.80 for women who used 0.5–1.5 standard (325 mg) tablets per week.
source: In particular, the dose-dependence of colorectal adenoma was studied (Chan et al., 2004), and it was shown that the relative risk for adenoma was 0.80 for women who used 0.5–1.5 standard (325 mg) tablets per week, 0.74 for those who used 2–5 tablets per week, 0.72 for those who used 6–14 tablets per week, and 0.49 for those who used more than 14 tablets per week.
evidence: This is data from Chan et al., 2004.

claim: The relative risk for adenoma was 0.74 for women who used 2–5 tablets per week.
source: In particular, the dose-dependence of colorectal adenoma was studied (Chan et al., 2004), and it was shown that the relative risk for adenoma was 0.80 for women who used 0.5–1.5 standard (325 mg) tablets per week, 0.74 for those who used 2–5 tablets per week, 0.72 for those who used 6–14 tablets per week, and 0.49 for those who used more than 14 tablets per week.
evidence: This is data from Chan et al., 2004.

claim: The relative risk for adenoma was 0.72 for women who used 6–14 tablets per week.
source: In particular, the dose-dependence of colorectal adenoma was studied (Chan et al., 2004), and it was shown that the relative risk for adenoma was 0.80 for women who used 0.5–1.5 standard (325 mg) tablets per week, 0.74 for those who used 2–5 tablets per week, 0.72 for those who used 6–14 tablets per week, and 0.49 for those who used more than 14 tablets per week.
evidence: This is data from Chan et al., 2004.

claim: The relative risk for adenoma was 0.49 for women who used more than 14 tablets per week.
source: In particular, the dose-dependence of colorectal adenoma was studied (Chan et al., 2004), and it was shown that the relative risk for adenoma was 0.80 for women who used 0.5–1.5 standard (325 mg) tablets per week, 0.74 for those who used 2–5 tablets per week, 0.72 for those who used 6–14 tablets per week, and 0.49 for those who used more than 14 tablets per week.
evidence: This is data from Chan et al., 2004.

claim: Aspirin had a negative impact on colon organoids derived from non-neoplastic tissues.
source: Interestingly, it has been shown that aspirin had a negative impact on colon organoids derived from non-neoplastic issues, and that aspirin particularly reduced the rapidly cycling transit amplifying cell population (Devall et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Devall et al., 2021.

claim: Aspirin particularly reduced the rapidly cycling transit amplifying cell population.
source: Interestingly, it has been shown that aspirin had a negative impact on colon organoids derived from non-neoplastic issues, and that aspirin particularly reduced the rapidly cycling transit amplifying cell population (Devall et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Devall et al., 2021.

claim: The model assumes that the removal rate of SCs is comprised of 90% differentiation and 10% apoptosis.
source: To calculate the fitness factor, we assumed that the removal rate of SCs, d, is comprised of 90% differentiation and 10% apoptosis, and that it is the latter that is affected by aspirin.
evidence: This is an explicit modeling assumption.

claim: Aspirin affects the apoptosis component of SC removal but not the differentiation component.
source: To calculate the fitness factor, we assumed that the removal rate of SCs, d, is comprised of 90% differentiation and 10% apoptosis, and that it is the latter that is affected by aspirin.
evidence: This is an explicit modeling assumption.

claim: The model assumes that under aspirin treatment, crypt fission rates are reduced and crypt death rates are increased.
source: In addition to affecting cellular fitness within the crypts, it is also logical to assume that aspirin reduces crypt fission rates and increases crypt death rates (the bottom row of the table in Figure 4(a)). This is supported by data (Fischer et al., 2014), and the rationale behind this assumption is that crypt fission is ultimately connected with divisions of individual cells, and crypt death is associated with cell death.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption supported by data from Fischer et al., 2014.

claim: Crypt fission is ultimately connected with divisions of individual cells.
source: This is supported by data (Fischer et al., 2014), and the rationale behind this assumption is that crypt fission is ultimately connected with divisions of individual cells, and crypt death is associated with cell death.
evidence: This is a biological rationale for the modeling assumption.

claim: Crypt death is associated with cell death.
source: This is supported by data (Fischer et al., 2014), and the rationale behind this assumption is that crypt fission is ultimately connected with divisions of individual cells, and crypt death is associated with cell death.
evidence: This is a biological rationale for the modeling assumption.

claim: The study used advanced adenoma incidence data from Brenner et al., 2014 for age-ranges 55–59, 60–64, 65–69, 70–74, and 75–79.
source: In order to study the incidence of advanced adenoma, we used the data reported in Brenner et al., 2014 for the age-ranges 55–59, 60–64, 65–69, 70–74, and 75–79.
evidence: This describes the data source used for model fitting.

claim: The study focused only on the combined incidence of advanced adenoma and cancer.
source: While this study provides incidence data for nonadvanced adenoma, advanced adenoma, and colorectal cancer (CRC), we focused only on the combined incidence of advanced adenoma and cancer.
evidence: This is an explicit methodological choice.

claim: Individuals that have developed CRC have most likely already developed an advanced adenoma by the age of testing.
source: This assumes that individuals that have developed CRC have most likely already developed an advanced adenoma by the age of testing, and further that nonadvanced adenoma likely refers to fewer mutational steps compared to our type 6, where both the APC gene is fully inactivated and the KRAS gene is mutated.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption based on the adenoma-carcinoma sequence.
